content: Invasive cervical carcinoma is preceded by a precancerous condition known as cervical intra-epithelial neoplasia (CIN). This condition can be identified through cervical smears and confirmed using colposcopy and biopsy. Moderate and severe forms of CIN, specifically CIN2 and CIN3, are typically managed with surgical interventions to prevent progression to invasive carcinoma. However, there is a need for medical treatments that can either halt the progression or induce the regression of CIN. Retinoids, which are potent regulators of epithelial cell growth and differentiation, have been proposed as potential therapeutic agents for CIN. The objective of this review was to determine whether retinoids can induce regression or prevent the progression of CIN. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Gynaecological Cancer Review Group's Specialised Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, and Embase, with updates performed in 2010, 2013, and 2015. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and non-RCTs that evaluated the use of retinoids in women with CIN. Two independent reviewers assessed the quality of the trials and extracted relevant data, including information on adverse effects. Five RCTs were identified, which evaluated the efficacy of four different retinoids. Two studies investigated the effects of oral administration of N-(4-hydroxyphenyl)retinamide (fenretinide) and 9-cis-retinoic acid (aliretinoin) on CIN2 and CIN3. Two other studies examined the topical application of all-trans-retinoic acid to the cervix. The fifth study evaluated the oral use of 13-cis-retinoic acid (isotretinoin) in HIV-positive participants with CIN1 and condyloma. Four of the studies found no significant effect of retinoids on the progression of CIN to higher grades. The fifth study did not report data on progression. None of the studies demonstrated a significant effect of retinoids on the regression of CIN3. However, two studies reported some association between retinoids and regression of CIN2. One of these studies showed a borderline statistically significant increase in complete regression of CIN2 compared to placebo (odds ratio [OR] 0.5, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.25 to 1.02). The other study reported a nonsignificant dose-related trend toward increased rates of complete and partial regression compared to placebo. Conversely, one study reported significantly worse outcomes in women treated with retinoids (OR for regression 6.00, 95% CI 1.00 to 35.91). Overall, retinoid medications were generally well tolerated at the doses and durations studied. However, no new studies were identified in the 2010, 2013, and 2015 updates, and the review was marked as stable. In conclusion, the retinoids studied do not appear to be effective in inducing regression of CIN3 and have limited evidence of efficacy in CIN2. There is insufficient data regarding their effects on CIN1. Furthermore, retinoids do not prevent the progression of CIN at any grade. At the doses and durations studied, retinoids were reasonably well tolerated.
